chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Utba, from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him: 'I have relatives upon whom I spend, and I prefer some of them over others. When the time for Zakat comes, should I give them from it?' He said: 'Are they entitled to it?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'They are better than others; give them from it.'

I said: 'Then who among my relatives must I support so that I do not count the Zakat as a debt owed to them?' He said: 'Your father and your mother.' I said: 'Your father and your mother?' He said: 'The parents and the children.'
ai.seo_question: Can I give my Zakat to my relatives, and does it matter if I am already supporting them?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) clarifies the distinction between voluntary charity (Sadaqah) and obligatory Zakat by excluding those upon whom one bears a mandatory financial duty, specifically parents and children, as their support is a separate obligation (Nafaqah). This ruling ensures that Zakat is reserved for eligible recipients who do not have a direct claim on the giver's wealth, a principle deeply rooted in Shia jurisprudence to prevent double-counting of charitable acts. The hadith highlights the precise categorization of Zakat recipients, emphasizing that eligibility depends on both their status as poor/needy and their lack of existing financial dependency on the giver.
